source.title: Explaining neural scaling laws
source.authors: Yasaman Bahri; Ethan Dyer; J. Kaplan; Jaehoon Lee; Utkarsh Sharma

record.tranche_reason: The study reports double-descent behavior in pretrained linear-feature models, a different model class and setup from the deep-network claim.
record.gate_note: The paper's asymptotic scaling results and its cited double-descent findings from other work are not rows. The relevant original results are the paper's own low- and tuned-regularization sweeps of dataset size and feature size in pretrained EfficientNet-B5 features (Figures S6 and S7).
record.test_reason: In Appendix F, the study's own kernel ridge regression sweeps on pretrained EfficientNet-B5 features show double descent at low regularization. This bears on V4 (a non-deep linear model class) and V3 (a dataset-size sweep). It is a side observation in a scaling-laws paper, shown only in figures, so T3 (new setting) fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The paper's main conclusion is a taxonomy of four scaling regimes (variance-limited and resolution-limited, in D and P) with a dataset/feature duality. Double descent appears only as a side remark: low regularization (late training) on pretrained features shows a double descent resonance at D = P, while tuned regularization corresponds to optimal early stopping. The authors do not explicitly claim the peak vanishes there.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines scaling in pretrained linear features and their regularization dependence, rather than reproducing the original deep-network double-descent experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper distinguishes fixed low regularization (long training time) from tuned regularization (optimal early stopping); it reports double-descent behavior for the low-regularization setting.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
record.problems: The double-descent curves are shown in figures without numerical values in the text. For the tuned-regularization curves, the text does not state whether the peak remains or disappears.

untested.parts: No deep-network test error swept over model size through an interpolation peak.
No test-error curve over training epochs (regularization is only mapped to inverse training time, not swept as epochs).
No deep-network sample-size sweep; only a linear model on fixed pretrained features.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Label noise is not varied and triple/multiple descent is not examined. Whether the peak disappears under tuned regularization is not stated.
No re-expression against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Authors attribute the deviation of the fitted variance-limited exponent from 1 at low regularization to 'the double descent resonance at D = P'. This locates the peak at D = P for both sweeps, and the row notes could quote it.
missing.locator: Appendix F, text discussing Figure S7

record.verdict_notes: Evidence for double descent is a caption statement plus one speculative sentence; no peak magnitudes are given. Sample-wise double descent [51] is only cited as an instance of the duality and is not a row. Verdicts rest on the authors' wording, not on read-off values.

versions.untested_parts: No test of a deep network's test error across model sizes through the interpolation peak.
No test-error curve over training epochs.
The reported data-scaling sweep is in pretrained linear-feature models, not a deep-network training-set-size sweep.
The tested feature model is a linear classifier on pretrained features; the paper does not test a broad range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.
The study varies regularization but does not test label-noise or variance as the peak's cause, or triple/multiple descent.
No curve is re-expressed against an appropriate effective parameter count.
